newsitem.title: USA: U.S. experts question Ecuador econ plan specifics.
newsitem.headline: U.S. experts question Ecuador econ plan specifics.

text.p: Ecuador's interim government may be developing a viable economic plan, but questions linger about its willingness to implement certain austerity measures, U.S. investors and analysts said Tuesday.
U.S. experts said they gained little new insight from Ecuador's economic leaders, who came to New York Monday to discuss their goal of reducing the public deficit.
After the presentation, experts said they still had questions on specifics, including plans for gasoline and cooking gas prices and government-sector wages.

"I don't know how effective the public relations campaign of this conference was, but I do know the key issues are still pending," said Siobhan Manning, senior Latin America analyst at Santander Investments.
Specifically, Manning said she had hoped to learn how the government would treat prices of gasoline and cooking gas and handle wages of government workers.
"The key issues were ones they didn't want to discuss -- what additional fiscal measures would be taken from here," she said.

In their presentation, central bank and ministry of finance officials said steps had already been approved to trim $795 million from the deficit by cutting spending and boosting income by roughly equal amounts.
"Their plan listed about 10 somewhat vague, but still revenue-raising, ideas," said Michael Henry, an economist at ING Barings.
Ecuador's proposals to reduce spending were even less specific, Henry said. "It would be hard to say exactly where they plan to cut and if those cuts are appropriate and feasible," he said.
But the fact that Ecuador's economic leadership has stepped outside the country to meet with investors suggested the government remained committed to economic reform, some Ecuador experts said.
"An under-developed country like Ecuador can't afford to have the 2.0-percent growth it's had on average over the last couple of years," one portfolio manager said.
The money manager called the evolving economic plan "realistic" but "moderate."
"You would expect that from an interim government. It's not the same kind of mandate you would have if you'd won a regular election," he said.

Ecuador hopes to achieve a standby loan agreement with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) by late 1997, a finance ministry official told reporters on Monday. Economic reforms are seen as key to reaching the agreement.
